subject: Anatomy
q: During excision of the submandibular gland, the lingual nerve is at risk of injury because it:
opts: Runs parallel and lateral to Wharton's duct throughout its course
Hooks below, then crosses medial to, the submandibular duct
Lies within the fibrous capsule of the gland itself
why: The nerve does not stay lateral throughout — it crosses the duct
Correct — hooks below and crosses medial to the duct
Piercing mylohyoid describes a different relation, not the duct-crossing risk
The nerve is not enclosed within the gland's capsule
exp: The lingual nerve lies medial to the mandible above the duct, then hooks below and crosses medial to (deep to) Wharton's duct near the second molar before ascending to the tongue; this crossing point puts the nerve at risk during gland/duct surgery.

subject: Anatomy
q: Below the arcuate line (linea semicircularis) of the rectus sheath:
opts: Both anterior and posterior layers of the rectus sheath are present
The inferior epigastric vessels are absent
Only transversalis fascia lies posterior to rectus abdominis; the posterior rectus sheath is deficient
The rectus abdominis muscle itself is absent
why: Above the arcuate line both layers are present; the question concerns below it
The vessels are still present, just more exposed
Correct — only transversalis fascia lies posterior below the line
Rectus abdominis continues to its pubic insertion
exp: Below the arcuate line, the posterior layer of internal oblique and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis both move anterior to the rectus abdominis, so only transversalis fascia and peritoneum lie posterior to the muscle — this is why the inferior epigastric vessels there are relatively unprotected and are used as a free-flap pedicle.

subject: Anatomy
q: The sural nerve, commonly harvested as a graft in nerve reconstruction, is formed by the union of:
opts: Tibial and common peroneal nerves directly, in the thigh
Medial sural cutaneous nerve and the peroneal communicating branch
why: Plantar nerves are terminal tibial nerve branches in the foot, unrelated
Tibial and common peroneal nerves diverge in the popliteal fossa but do not themselves form the sural nerve
The saphenous nerve is a separate femoral nerve branch
Correct — medial sural cutaneous nerve plus peroneal communicating branch
exp: The sural nerve is formed in the calf by union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve) with the peroneal communicating branch (from the common peroneal nerve); its purely sensory territory makes it a favoured donor graft with acceptable sensory deficit.

subject: Anatomy
q: Structures derived from the cartilage (Reichert's cartilage) of the second pharyngeal arch include:
opts: Stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, and lesser horn of hyoid
Greater horn and body of hyoid
why: Correct — classic second-arch (Reichert's cartilage) derivatives
Malleus and incus derive from the first arch (Meckel's cartilage)
Thyroid and cricoid cartilages derive from the fourth/sixth arches
Greater horn and lower hyoid body derive from the third arch
exp: Reichert's cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch (supplied by CN VII) forms the stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, and the lesser horn plus upper part of the hyoid body.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus senses luminal sodium chloride concentration?
opts: Macula densa of the distal convoluted tubule
Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells of the afferent arteriole
why: Extraglomerular mesangial cells relay the signal but are not the primary sensor
Correct — senses distal tubular NaCl/chloride concentration
JG cells secrete renin in response to the macula densa signal but do not sense NaCl themselves
Podocytes form the filtration slit diaphragm, unrelated to NaCl sensing
exp: The macula densa is a group of specialized distal convoluted tubule cells at the junction with the afferent arteriole that senses luminal NaCl concentration; low delivery triggers renin secretion from the juxtaglomerular cells (tubuloglomerular feedback).

subject: Anatomy
q: The carotid sheath, formed by all three layers of deep cervical fascia, encloses which structures?
opts: External carotid artery, external jugular vein, hypoglossal nerve
Common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, phrenic nerve
Common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve
Internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and the cervical sympathetic chain
why: External carotid artery and external jugular vein lie outside the sheath
The phrenic nerve runs on prevertebral fascia over scalenus anterior, outside the sheath
Correct — common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve
The sympathetic chain lies posterior to, not within, the sheath
exp: The carotid sheath encloses the common (and internal) carotid artery, the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve; the cervical sympathetic chain runs just posterior to, but outside, the sheath.

subject: Anatomy
q: During splenectomy, ligation of the splenic vessels close to the splenic hilum carries the highest risk of injury to which structure?
why: The left kidney is related to the spleen but not directly endangered by hilar vessel ligation
The greater curvature/short gastric vessels are a separate splenectomy risk, not from hilar ligation
The splenic flexure relates to the inferior pole of the spleen, not the vascular hilum
Correct — the pancreatic tail is at risk at the splenic hilum
exp: The tail of the pancreas often reaches close to the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament alongside the splenic vessels, so blind mass ligation of the vessels at the hilum risks pancreatic tail injury and postoperative pancreatic fistula.

subject: Anatomy
q: Sensory supply to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords is provided by which nerve?
why: Too non-specific; named branches carry the distinct functions
Correct - sensory above the vocal folds
Sensory below the vocal folds, motor to intrinsic muscles
Motor to cricothyroid only, not sensory
exp: The internal laryngeal nerve (branch of the superior laryngeal nerve) pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to supply sensation to the laryngeal mucosa down to the vocal folds; below this, sensation is via the recurrent laryngeal nerve - why foreign bodies above the cords trigger a strong cough reflex.

subject: Anatomy
q: The greater curvature of the stomach receives its arterial supply mainly from which pair of arteries?
why: Supply the lesser curvature, not the greater
Too general; the specific vessels are the gastroepiploics
Correct - run along and supply the greater curvature
Supply the fundus, from the splenic artery
exp: The right gastroepiploic (from gastroduodenal artery) and left gastroepiploic (from splenic artery) anastomose along the greater curvature - relevant when planning a gastric conduit or omental flap.

subject: Anatomy
q: Injury to the tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa results in loss of which movement at the ankle?
why: Lost with common peroneal nerve injury, not tibial
Supplied by the femoral nerve, unaffected
Correct - tibial nerve supplies the plantarflexors
Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, unaffected
exp: The tibial nerve supplies the posterior leg compartment; injury at the popliteal fossa paralyses the plantarflexors (gastrocnemius, soleus), producing a calcaneovalgus deformity - contrast with common peroneal nerve injury, which causes foot drop from loss of dorsiflexion.

subject: Anatomy
q: Failure of fusion of the urogenital folds in the male fetus results in which congenital anomaly?
why: A more severe midline cloacal membrane defect
Results from abnormal genital tubercle positioning, not fold fusion failure
Correct - failure of urogenital fold fusion
Defect of infra-umbilical mesenchyme/cloacal membrane
exp: Hypospadias results from incomplete fusion of the urogenital folds on the ventral penis, leaving the urethral meatus opening proximal to its normal tip position; epispadias instead reflects abnormal genital tubercle positioning relative to the urorectal septum.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which testicular cell type secretes testosterone in response to LH stimulation?
why: Correct - respond to LH and synthesize testosterone
Respond to FSH, support spermatogenesis, don't secrete testosterone
Germ cells, not hormone-secreting
Contractile cells aiding sperm transport, not steroidogenic
exp: Leydig (interstitial) cells, in the connective tissue between seminiferous tubules, synthesize testosterone in response to LH; Sertoli cells, by contrast, respond to FSH, form the blood-testis barrier, and nurture spermatogonia - a commonly confused pair.

subject: Anatomy
q: Injury to which cranial nerve during tonsillectomy classically causes loss of the gag reflex and taste on the posterior third of the tongue?
why: Contributes to the gag reflex efferent limb, not this sensory loss
Correct - supplies posterior tongue and gag afferent limb, near tonsillar bed
Purely motor to the tongue, no sensory/gag role
Supplies facial muscles/anterior tongue taste, unrelated to tonsillar bed
exp: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies general and taste sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex; it runs close to the tonsillar bed, so tonsillectomy or peritonsillar abscess drainage can injure it.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structure normally occupies the femoral canal, and predisposes it to being the site of a femoral hernia?
opts: Lymph node of Cloquet (deep inguinal lymph node)
why: Femoral artery lies in the lateral compartment of the sheath, not the canal
Femoral vein occupies the intermediate compartment, not the medial canal
Femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral sheath entirely, outside it
Correct — Cloquet's node sits in the femoral canal, the compartment femoral hernias push through
exp: The femoral sheath's three compartments run lateral to medial as artery-vein-canal (NAVeL); the medial-most femoral canal is normally empty except for loose fat and the deep inguinal (Cloquet's) lymph node — precisely this emptiness is why it becomes the space a femoral hernia pushes through.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossa?
why: Levator ani forms the medial wall/roof of the fossa, not the lateral wall
Piriformis is a pelvic wall muscle above the pelvic floor, unrelated to the ischioanal fossa boundaries
Correct — obturator internus and its fascia form the lateral wall
Gluteus maximus lies outside/posterior to the fossa, overlying it superficially but not forming a wall
exp: The ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossa is a fat-filled wedge bounded medially by levator ani/external anal sphincter and laterally by obturator internus muscle with its covering fascia — the same fascia carries the pudendal canal, and this fossa's continuity across the midline explains horseshoe abscess spread.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which type of epithelium lines the vagina and the ectocervix?
why: Correct — vagina and ectocervix are non-keratinized stratified squamous
Simple columnar epithelium lines the endocervix, not vagina/ectocervix
Transitional epithelium lines the urinary tract, unrelated to the vagina
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium lines the fallopian tube and respiratory tract, not the vagina
exp: Vagina and ectocervix are lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, switching to simple columnar epithelium at the squamocolumnar junction of the endocervix — the site most relevant to cervical dysplasia and cancer screening.

subject: Anatomy
q: How far above the medial third of the clavicle does the cervical pleura/apex of the lung typically extend into the root of the neck?
opts: It does not extend above the clavicle
why: 1 cm underestimates the standard teaching value
Correct — the classical figure taught is ~2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle
5 cm overstates the extent implausibly
The apex does project above the clavicle, which is exactly why supraclavicular procedures carry pneumothorax risk
exp: The apex of the lung and its overlying cervical pleura project roughly 2.5 cm above the medial third of the clavicle into the root of the neck — clinically relevant because it puts the lung apex at risk during supraclavicular procedures, risking pneumothorax.

subject: Anatomy
q: The free margin of the falciform ligament (the ligamentum teres hepatis) is the fibrous remnant of which fetal structure?
why: Ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum near the aortic arch, unrelated to the falciform ligament
Urachus becomes the median umbilical ligament from bladder to umbilicus, not in the falciform ligament
Vitelline duct remnants relate to Meckel's diverticulum, not the falciform ligament
Correct — ligamentum teres hepatis is the obliterated left umbilical vein
exp: The ligamentum teres hepatis, carried in the free edge of the falciform ligament, is the obliterated remnant of the fetal left umbilical vein; recanalization of this vein in portal hypertension produces caput medusae.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which thigh muscle characteristically receives dual innervation from both the femoral and obturator nerves?
why: Sartorius is supplied solely by the femoral nerve
Adductor longus is supplied solely by the obturator nerve
Correct — pectineus classically has dual femoral and obturator innervation
Gracilis is supplied solely by the obturator nerve
exp: Pectineus is unusual among thigh muscles in receiving a dual nerve supply — mainly the femoral nerve, with a variable additional twig from the obturator nerve — reflecting its position at the boundary of the anterior and medial thigh compartments.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to part of the external auditory canal and can cause referred ear pain in disorders of the larynx and pharynx?
why: Auriculotemporal (from mandibular nerve) supplies anterior canal but is not the vagal referred-pain route
Great auricular supplies the auricle's skin, a cervical plexus branch, not linked to laryngopharyngeal referral
Correct - vagal auricular branch, explains referred otalgia
Lesser occipital supplies scalp behind the ear, unrelated to canal sensation
exp: Arnold's nerve, the auricular branch of the vagus, supplies part of the external auditory canal; because the vagus also supplies the larynx and pharynx, disease there can cause referred otalgia via this shared nerve.

subject: Anatomy
q: The appendicular artery, which supplies the vermiform appendix, is a branch of which artery?
why: The SMA gives rise to the ileocolic artery, which in turn gives the appendicular artery - not a direct branch
The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon, not the appendix
The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut structures (descending colon, sigmoid, rectum), unrelated to the appendix
Correct - the ileocolic artery (a branch of the SMA) gives rise to the appendicular artery, an end artery predisposing to rapid gangrene in appendicitis
exp: The appendicular artery is a branch of the ileocolic artery (itself from the SMA) and runs in the mesoappendix; it is functionally an end artery with poor collateral supply, explaining why appendiceal ischemia and gangrene occur rapidly once flow is compromised in acute appendicitis.

subject: Anatomy
q: Injury to which nerve, as it winds around the neck of the fibula, produces foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion?
why: Tibial nerve injury causes loss of plantarflexion/inversion, not foot drop
Saphenous nerve is purely sensory (medial leg), no motor loss
Sural nerve is purely sensory (lateral foot/calf)
Correct - classic fibular-neck vulnerability and foot drop
exp: The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, making it vulnerable to compression, and its loss produces the classic foot drop with high-stepping gait.

subject: Anatomy
q: The oblique fissure of the right lung, when traced onto the surface of the chest wall, most closely corresponds to which surface landmark?
opts: A line from the spinous process of T2 to the 6th costal cartilage
A line from the spinous process of T3 to the 6th costal cartilage, crossing the 5th rib in the mid-axillary line
The 4th intercostal space anteriorly on both sides
A horizontal line at the level of the 4th costal cartilage
why: Wrong starting vertebral level (T2, not T3)
Correct - standard oblique fissure surface marking
Describes the horizontal fissure region, not the oblique fissure
Horizontal fissure on the right runs roughly at the 4th costal cartilage anteriorly, not this description
exp: The oblique fissure surface marking runs from the spinous process of T3 posteriorly, crosses the 5th rib in the mid-axillary line, and reaches the 6th costal cartilage anteriorly - used to plan chest tube placement.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which cell type in the seminiferous tubule forms the blood-testis barrier via tight junctions and provides structural/nutritional support to developing spermatozoa?
why: Leydig cells lie in the interstitium and produce testosterone, unrelated to the barrier
Correct - Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier
Spermatogonia are the germ cells protected by, not forming, the barrier
Peritubular myoid cells contract to move sperm/fluid but do not form the tight-junction barrier
exp: Sertoli cells form tight junctional complexes between adjacent cells that create the blood-testis barrier, compartmentalising the tubule to protect developing germ cells and provide androgen-binding protein support.

subject: Anatomy
q: The pterygopalatine ganglion, which mediates lacrimation and nasal gland secretion, receives its parasympathetic root from which nerve?
why: Deep petrosal carries sympathetic fibres, joining the greater petrosal to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal
Correct - parasympathetic root of the pterygopalatine ganglion
Lesser petrosal carries parasympathetics to the otic ganglion for the parotid gland, a different ganglion
Auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion to the parotid, unrelated here
exp: The greater petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the facial nerve to the pterygopalatine ganglion, explaining crocodile tears syndrome after aberrant facial nerve regeneration.

subject: Anatomy
q: The facial nerve trunk divides within the substance of the parotid gland to form the parotid plexus, giving rise to five terminal motor branches supplying the muscles of facial expression. Which of the following is NOT one of these five terminal branches?
why: Correct — the auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, not a facial nerve branch.
Wrong — a genuine terminal branch of the facial nerve.
Wrong — a genuine terminal branch of the facial nerve.
Wrong — a genuine terminal branch of the facial nerve.
exp: The parotid gland is traversed by the facial nerve (motor), which divides into 5 terminal branches (mnemonic: Two Zebras Bit My Cat — Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical), while the auriculotemporal nerve is a trigeminal branch whose aberrant regeneration after parotid injury causes Frey's syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
q: A thin young woman presents with recurrent postprandial vomiting and epigastric pain relieved by lying prone or in the knee-chest position. Imaging shows the third part of the duodenum compressed between which two structures, causing her symptoms?
opts: The aorta and the inferior vena cava
The superior mesenteric artery and the aorta
The pancreas and the transverse colon
The right renal artery and the right renal vein
why: Wrong — the IVC is not the compressing structure in this syndrome.
Correct — SMA syndrome compresses the third part of the duodenum between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.
Wrong — not the compressing structures in this syndrome.
Wrong — renal vessel compression describes nutcracker syndrome, a different entity.
exp: SMA syndrome results from a narrowed aortomesenteric angle due to loss of the mesenteric fat pad, compressing the third part of duodenum; the knee-chest or left lateral decubitus position relieves symptoms by increasing this angle.

subject: Anatomy
q: A patient develops severe pain, pallor, and paresthesia of the leg after a tibial fracture, with pain markedly worsened on passive plantarflexion of the toes/ankle. Compartment pressure is elevated in the anterior compartment of the leg. Which nerve is most at risk of injury within this compartment?
why: Wrong — runs in the lateral compartment.
Wrong — runs in the posterior compartment.
Correct — the deep peroneal nerve runs within the anterior compartment and is at greatest risk in anterior compartment syndrome.
Wrong — a superficial sensory nerve in the posterior/lateral leg, not the anterior compartment.
exp: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, pallor, pulselessness as a late sign) requiring emergency fasciotomy; the anterior compartment is the most commonly affected after tibial fractures.

subject: Anatomy
q: An unconscious patient aspirates gastric contents while supine. The aspirated material is most likely to lodge in which bronchopulmonary segment, given the anatomical course of the right main bronchus?
opts: Apical segment of the left upper lobe
Lingular segment of the left upper lobe
Anterior basal segment of the left lower lobe
Superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe
why: Wrong — the left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal, making left-sided aspiration less common.
Wrong — the left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal, making left-sided aspiration less common.
Wrong — a plausible site in upright or semi-recumbent posture, not supine.
Correct — the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, and the superior segment of the right lower lobe is the classic dependent site in a supine patient.
exp: The right main bronchus's wider, shorter, more vertical course explains why aspiration occurs more often on the right; the exact dependent segment involved varies with patient position.

subject: Anatomy
q: On light microscopy of a pancreatic section, an islet of Langerhans is examined. Which cell type is most numerous, located predominantly in the central portion of the islet, and stains for insulin?
why: Correct — beta cells (about 60-70% of islet cells) are the most numerous, centrally located, insulin-secreting cells.
Wrong — alpha cells (about 20-25%), peripheral, secrete glucagon.
Wrong — delta cells (about 5-10%), scattered, secrete somatostatin.
Wrong — a minority population secreting pancreatic polypeptide.
exp: Islet of Langerhans cytoarchitecture classically shows beta cells (insulin) dominating centrally, with alpha (glucagon), delta (somatostatin), and PP cells at the periphery — this spatial arrangement supports paracrine regulation between cell types.

subject: Anatomy
q: During carotid endarterectomy, a surgeon needs to distinguish the internal carotid artery from the external carotid artery in the neck. Which feature reliably identifies the internal carotid artery?
opts: It gives off multiple branches within the neck
It gives off no branches in the neck (ascends to enter the carotid canal without branching)
It is more medially and superficially placed than the external carotid
It supplies the thyroid gland directly
why: Wrong — describes the external carotid artery.
Correct — the internal carotid artery characteristically gives off no branches in the neck.
Wrong — position is a less reliable distinguishing feature than the branching pattern.
Wrong — the superior thyroid artery, an external carotid branch, supplies the thyroid.
exp: The single most reliable operative distinction between ICA and ECA is that the ICA has no branches in the neck while the ECA gives off multiple named branches — useful when ligating vessels during neck surgery or trauma, since inadvertent ICA ligation risks stroke.

subject: Anatomy
q: In a patient with portal hypertension, dilated tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae) result from a portosystemic anastomosis between the portal venous system and the:
opts: Paraumbilical veins communicating with superficial epigastric veins (via the ligamentum teres)
Left gastric vein and the azygos vein
Superior rectal vein and the middle/inferior rectal veins
Splenic vein and the left renal vein
why: Correct - this is the specific anastomosis producing caput medusae
Left gastric-azygos anastomosis produces oesophageal varices, a different clinical sign
Superior rectal-middle/inferior rectal anastomosis produces haemorrhoids, not caput medusae

There is no clinically significant splenic-left renal portosystemic anastomosis taught as a classic site (splenorenal shunts are surgically created, not a natural anastomosis producing a clinical sign)
exp: Caput medusae forms when portal hypertension reopens the paraumbilical veins running in the ligamentum teres (the obliterated umbilical vein), which anastomose with the superficial and inferior epigastric veins of the anterior abdominal wall, draining into the systemic caval system - a distinct portosystemic site from oesophageal varices (left gastric-azygos) or haemorrhoids (rectal venous plexus).

subject: Anatomy
q: A 70-year-old woman presents with pain along the medial thigh extending to the knee, worsened by extension, abduction, and medial rotation of the hip. Which nerve entrapment, classically associated with obturator hernia, best explains this finding?
why: Correct - the obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal and is compressed by an obturator hernia, producing medial thigh pain (Howship-Romberg sign)
Femoral nerve compression causes anterior thigh pain and weak knee extension, not this pattern
Sciatic nerve compression causes posterior thigh/leg pain and foot drop, unrelated to the hip-movement trigger described
Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh compression causes meralgia paresthetica (lateral thigh burning), not medial thigh pain
exp: Howship-Romberg sign is pain along the medial thigh to the knee from obturator nerve compression by an obturator hernia, worsened by hip extension, abduction, or medial rotation, classically in thin, elderly, multiparous women.

subject: Anatomy
q: A 40-year-old man with a perianal abscess develops bilateral gluteal swelling and fever. Imaging shows pus tracking posteriorly across the midline. Through which anatomical space does infection typically spread to form this horseshoe abscess?
opts: Ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa via the deep postanal space
why: Superficial perineal pouch is bounded by Colles fascia and is the plane for extravasated urine, not perianal sepsis spread
Rectovesical pouch is a peritoneal reflection unrelated to perianal spaces
Correct - the deep postanal space connects the two ischioanal fossae, allowing pus to track across the midline and form a horseshoe abscess
Denonvilliers fascia separates rectum from prostate/seminal vesicles, not involved in ischioanal spread
exp: The deep postanal space (of Courtney) lies below levator ani and above the anococcygeal ligament, and is the conduit that lets a perianal abscess spread to the contralateral ischioanal fossa, forming a horseshoe abscess.

subject: Anatomy
q: A neonate is born with loose loops of bowel protruding through a paraumbilical abdominal wall defect, with no covering membrane and a normally inserted umbilical cord. Which embryological defect best explains this presentation?
opts: Failure of lateral body fold fusion with persistent extraembryonic coelom
Abnormal involution of the right umbilical vein leading to a paraumbilical defect
why: This describes omphalocele pathogenesis - a midline defect at the cord itself with a peritoneal sac, not this case
Vitelline duct persistence causes Meckel diverticulum or an umbilical fistula, not an abdominal wall defect
A urachal remnant causes umbilical discharge or cyst, not bowel herniation
Correct - this vascular insult is the commonly taught mechanism for gastroschisis, a paraumbilical defect with no covering sac and a normally inserted cord
exp: Gastroschisis (bowel through a paraumbilical defect, no sac, normally inserted cord) is taught as arising from a vascular insult weakening the lateral body wall, distinct from omphalocele which is a failure of lateral fold fusion at the cord insertion itself. Exact vascular etiology is still debated in the literature.

subject: Anatomy
q: Six months after a parotidectomy, a patient reports facial sweating and flushing over the cheek whenever eating. Which nerve fibers are responsible for this phenomenon due to aberrant regeneration?
opts: Facial nerve motor fibers regenerating into cutaneous branches
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve regenerating to innervate sweat glands
Chorda tympani fibers reinnervating the submandibular gland
why: Facial nerve fiber misdirection causes synkinesis, not gustatory sweating
Correct - this is the mechanism of Frey syndrome after parotid surgery
Greater auricular nerve injury causes earlobe numbness, not sweating
Chorda tympani governs taste and submandibular/sublingual salivation, unrelated to Frey syndrome
exp: Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating) follows aberrant regeneration of parasympathetic secretomotor fibers, normally destined for the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve, into cutaneous sweat glands after parotid surgery.

subject: Anatomy
q: Regarding primary lumbar hernias, which anatomical triangle is the more common site of herniation, despite the inferior lumbar triangle (of Petit) being the more classically taught and illustrated location?
why: Petit's triangle is smaller, and less commonly the actual site of herniation despite being the more traditionally cited location
Correct - the superior lumbar triangle (Grynfeltt-Lesshaft), bounded by the 12th rib, internal oblique, and quadratus lumborum/erector spinae, is the more common site of primary lumbar hernia
Calot's triangle is in the hepatobiliary region, unrelated
Hesselbach's triangle relates to a direct inguinal hernia, not a lumbar hernia
exp: The superior lumbar triangle of Grynfeltt-Lesshaft is the more common site of primary lumbar hernia (roughly two-thirds of cases), even though the inferior triangle of Petit is the one most classically depicted in textbook diagrams.

subject: Anatomy
q: After an intramuscular injection given too medially in the gluteal region, a patient develops a lurching gait with pelvic drop on the opposite side while standing on the affected limb. Injury to which nerve best explains this Trendelenburg sign?
why: Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, causing difficulty rising from sitting or climbing stairs, not pelvic instability in stance
Pudendal nerve supplies perineal structures, unrelated to gait
Sciatic nerve injury causes hamstring weakness and foot drop, not primarily a Trendelenburg gait
Correct - the superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius/minimus, the hip abductors that stabilize the pelvis in single-limb stance
exp: Superior gluteal nerve injury, classically from a gluteal injection placed too medially or during hip surgery, causes a positive Trendelenburg sign due to weakness of gluteus medius and minimus.

subject: Anatomy
q: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through which foramen?
why: Jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI, not XII.
Foramen ovale transmits CN V3.
Stylomastoid foramen transmits the facial nerve (CN VII).
Correct - CN XII exits through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone.
exp: CN XII, supplying all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles except palatoglossus, exits via the hypoglossal canal just above and lateral to the foramen magnum - keep this distinct from the adjacent jugular foramen's CN IX/X/XI.

subject: Anatomy
q: Esophageal varices in portal hypertension develop due to a portosystemic anastomosis between the left gastric vein and which systemic vein?
why: Correct - the portal left gastric vein anastomoses with the systemic esophageal veins draining into the azygos system at the gastroesophageal junction.
Superior rectal vein anastomoses with rectal veins at the anal canal, a different site (hemorrhoids).
Paraumbilical veins anastomose with abdominal wall veins at the umbilicus (caput medusae), a different site.
Splenic vein is a portal tributary, not part of a portosystemic anastomosis itself.
exp: The gastroesophageal junction anastomosis is the highest-risk of the four classic portosystemic sites because of its submucosal location and high pressure, making esophageal varices the most dangerous manifestation of portal hypertension.

subject: Anatomy
q: The adductor canal (subsartorial/Hunter's canal) in the thigh transmits which structures?
opts: Sciatic nerve and profunda femoris artery
Femoral artery, femoral vein, and saphenous nerve
Obturator nerve and obturator artery only
why: The sciatic nerve and profunda femoris run in the posterior thigh, not the adductor canal.
Correct - the canal transmits the femoral artery and vein, and the saphenous nerve.
The obturator neurovascular bundle runs in the medial thigh but not within the canal itself.
The popliteal artery and tibial nerve are found in the popliteal fossa, distal to the canal.
exp: The adductor canal is a key surgical landmark for exposing the femoral vessels mid-thigh; the femoral vessels become the popliteal vessels after passing through the adductor hiatus at the canal's distal end.

subject: Anatomy
q: The notochord plays which key inductive role during early embryonic development?
opts: It gives rise to the definitive vertebral bodies
It induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate (primary neurulation)
It differentiates into the neural crest
why: Vertebral bodies form from sclerotome, not the notochord itself, though the notochord regresses within them.
The primitive streak forms earlier and gives rise to the notochord via the notochordal process, not the reverse.
Correct - the notochord signals overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate, the first step of neurulation.
The neural crest arises from the neural tube's lateral margins/ectoderm, not by direct differentiation of the notochord.
exp: Notochord-induced neural plate formation (primary neurulation) is the founding event of CNS development; the notochord itself regresses, persisting only as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which testicular cell type forms the blood-testis barrier and provides structural/nutritional support to developing sperm cells?
why: Leydig cells lie in the interstitium and produce testosterone, not the barrier/support function.
Spermatogonia are the germ cells being supported, not the supporting cells.
Peritubular myoid cells contribute to tubule contraction, not the blood-testis barrier.
Correct - Sertoli cell tight junctions form the blood-testis barrier, and Sertoli cells nurture developing germ cells throughout spermatogenesis.
exp: Sertoli cells create an immune-privileged compartment for maturing germ cells via the blood-testis barrier, and also secrete inhibin and androgen-binding protein - central to both endocrine and reproductive physiology questions on this topic.

subject: Anatomy
q: A midline neck swelling in a child that moves upward on tongue protrusion is most characteristic of which congenital anomaly?
why: Correct - a thyroglossal duct cyst remains tethered to the hyoid bone/tongue base, so it moves with tongue protrusion and swallowing.
Branchial cleft cysts are lateral neck swellings, not midline, and don't move with tongue protrusion.
Cystic hygroma is a lateral, transilluminant lymphatic malformation, usually in the posterior triangle.
A cervical rib presents with thoracic outlet symptoms, not a neck swelling that moves with the tongue.
exp: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the thyroid's embryological descent from the foramen cecum to its pretracheal position; movement with tongue protrusion is the classic clinical discriminator from a branchial cleft cyst.

subject: Anatomy
q: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct typically join and open into the duodenum at which site?
opts: Major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum
why: The duodenojejunal flexure is the distal end of the duodenum, unrelated to biliary/pancreatic drainage.
Correct - the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
The pylorus is the gastroduodenal junction, proximal to the ampulla.
The first part of the duodenum is proximal to the papilla, which is located in the second part.
exp: The major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi, is the key landmark for ERCP cannulation and the site of obstruction in a periampullary tumor causing painless jaundice.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which nerve is at particular risk of injury during a Lanz (gridiron) incision for open appendectomy, as it runs just deep to the muscle layers in the right iliac fossa?
opts: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
why: Correct — most commonly at risk in this incision
Genitofemoral nerve runs on psoas major, deeper and more medial
Iliohypogastric nerve lies slightly more superior and is less commonly injured here
This nerve runs more laterally near the anterior superior iliac spine, at risk in different approaches (e.g., hip surgery)
exp: The ilioinguinal nerve courses through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall in the right iliac fossa, close to the McBurney's point incision line, and can be injured or entrapped during appendectomy, causing groin numbness or chronic post-surgical neuralgia.

subject: Anatomy
q: Posterior dislocation of the hip joint classically places which nerve at risk of injury, presenting with foot drop and sensory loss below the knee?
why: Femoral nerve lies anteriorly and is not typically injured in posterior dislocation
Obturator nerve is medial and rarely involved
Correct — posteriorly placed and classically injured
Superior gluteal nerve injury is associated with iatrogenic injury during hip surgery approaches, not dislocation
exp: The sciatic nerve lies posterior to the hip joint capsule and is the nerve most commonly injured in posterior hip dislocation, with the common peroneal division typically affected preferentially, producing foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structure carries the ovarian artery, vein, and nerves from the pelvic wall to the ovary, and must be carefully identified during oophorectomy to avoid injuring the nearby ureter?
opts: Infundibulopelvic ligament (suspensory ligament of the ovary)
why: The broad ligament is the peritoneal fold in which the infundibulopelvic ligament lies, but it is not itself the vessel-carrying structure
Round ligament connects the uterus to the labium majus and carries no major vessels
Correct — carries the ovarian vessels near the ureter
Ovarian ligament proper connects ovary to uterus and carries no major named vessels
exp: The infundibulopelvic ligament (suspensory ligament of the ovary) is a peritoneal fold carrying the ovarian vessels and nerves from the pelvic side wall to the ovary; the ureter runs close to its base, making it a key structure to identify and safely ligate during oophorectomy or hysterectomy to prevent ureteric injury.

subject: Anatomy
q: The thoracic duct, draining lymph from the entire body except the right upper quadrant, empties into the venous system at which point?
opts: Junction of the right subclavian and right internal jugular veins
Junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins (left venous angle)
Directly into the inferior vena cava
why: This is the drainage site of the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct
Correct — the thoracic duct's termination point
The thoracic duct does not drain directly into the heart
The thoracic duct does not drain into the IVC
exp: The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle — the confluence of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins — while the smaller right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quadrant into the right venous angle.

subject: Anatomy
q: During ligation of the superior thyroid artery close to the superior pole of the thyroid gland, which nerve is at particular risk of injury, resulting in loss of voice pitch control if damaged?
why: Correct — closely applied to the superior thyroid vessels at the upper pole
RLN runs near the inferior thyroid artery and posterior to the gland, not the superior pole
Internal laryngeal nerve is sensory to the supraglottic larynx and lies deeper
The vagus trunk runs within the carotid sheath, well away from the superior pole
exp: The external laryngeal nerve (a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve) runs in close proximity to the superior thyroid artery near the gland's upper pole and supplies the cricothyroid muscle; injury impairs voice pitch modulation, unlike recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, which causes hoarseness and can compromise the airway.

subject: Anatomy
q: The anal canal above the pectinate (dentate) line is supplied by which artery, and below the line by which artery?
opts: Above: superior rectal artery; below: inferior rectal artery
Above: inferior rectal artery; below: superior rectal artery
Above and below both by the middle rectal artery alone
Above: internal pudendal artery; below: superior rectal artery
why: Correct — matches the embryological hindgut/proctodeum divide at the pectinate line
Reverses the correct arterial supply
The middle rectal artery contributes but is not the sole or primary supply to either zone
Internal pudendal artery gives rise to the inferior, not superior, rectal artery
exp: Above the pectinate line (embryologically hindgut-derived), the anal canal is supplied by the superior rectal artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery); below the line (proctodeum-derived), it is supplied by the inferior rectal artery (from the internal pudendal artery) — this divide also explains the differing venous drainage, lymphatic drainage, and innervation above and below the line.

subject: Anatomy
q: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the head of femur) transmits a branch of which artery, important as the primary blood supply to the femoral head in childhood?
why: Medial circumflex femoral artery is the dominant supply in adults via the retinacular vessels, not via the ligamentum teres
Superior gluteal artery does not supply the femoral head
Lateral circumflex femoral artery contributes minimally to femoral head supply
Correct — travels within the ligamentum teres
exp: The artery to the head of femur, a branch of the obturator artery, travels within the ligamentum teres and is the dominant blood supply to the femoral head in early childhood; in adults its contribution is minimal, and disruption of the retinacular vessels after femoral neck fracture is the major cause of avascular necrosis.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structure passes through the diaphragm at the T10 vertebral level, accompanied by the anterior and posterior vagal trunks?
why: IVC passes at T8, not T10
Aorta passes posterior to the diaphragm at T12
Correct — oesophageal hiatus at T10
Thoracic duct passes with the aorta at T12, not at the oesophageal hiatus
exp: The oesophageal opening in the diaphragm lies at the T10 level and transmits the oesophagus along with the anterior and posterior vagal trunks; the IVC passes through the central tendon at T8, while the aorta passes posterior to the diaphragm at T12.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which gastric mucosal cell type secretes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and whose autoimmune destruction causes pernicious anemia?
why: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not acid or intrinsic factor
Correct — the dual acid/intrinsic factor-secreting cell
Mucous neck cells secrete protective mucus
G cells (in the antrum) secrete gastrin, a hormone, not intrinsic factor
exp: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the gastric fundic glands secrete hydrochloric acid via the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump and intrinsic factor, essential for terminal ileal vitamin B12 absorption; autoimmune gastritis targeting parietal cells causes pernicious anaemia with B12 deficiency.

subject: Anatomy
q: Special taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by which nerve, even though it travels alongside the lingual nerve?
opts: Chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve)
why: Glossopharyngeal carries taste from the posterior one-third, not the anterior two-thirds
Correct — facial nerve's chorda tympani branch
Lingual nerve carries general sensation only, not taste
Hypoglossal is purely motor to the tongue musculature
exp: The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), joins the lingual nerve (CN V3) but carries special taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, while general sensation there is carried by the lingual nerve itself; taste from the posterior third is via the glossopharyngeal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
q: Compression of which nerve within the tarsal tunnel, posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, produces tarsal tunnel syndrome with burning pain and paresthesia in the sole of the foot?
why: The sural nerve supplies the lateral foot/ankle and runs posterolateral to the lateral malleolus, not through the tarsal tunnel.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies the dorsum of the foot and runs anterolaterally, unrelated to the tarsal tunnel.
Correct — the tibial nerve passes through the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus and is compressed in tarsal tunnel syndrome.
The deep peroneal nerve runs on the dorsum of the foot in the anterior compartment, not through the tarsal tunnel.
exp: The tarsal tunnel is formed by the flexor retinaculum stretching from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus, transmitting the tibial nerve along with tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus tendons — compression here causes burning pain/paresthesia over the sole via the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

subject: Anatomy
q: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) gland lies in the superficial perineal pouch and is the female homologue of which male structure?
why: The prostate is homologous to the paraurethral (Skene's) glands, not Bartholin's glands.
The seminal vesicle has no established female homologue in the standard embryological correspondence.
The epididymis is homologous to structures like the epoophoron, not Bartholin's glands.
Correct — Bartholin's glands are the female homologue of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.
exp: The greater vestibular glands lubricate the vestibule during arousal and lie posterolateral to the vaginal orifice in the superficial perineal pouch; they are embryologically and functionally homologous to the male bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands, which similarly secrete a lubricating mucus into the urethra before ejaculation.

subject: Anatomy
q: In hepatic acinar zonation, which zone is most susceptible to ischemic injury (as it receives the least oxygenated blood) but shows the highest cytochrome P450 drug-metabolizing activity?
why: Zone 1 (periportal) receives the most oxygenated blood first and is relatively protected from ischemia, being more susceptible instead to bile-duct-related or viral injury patterns.
Zone 2 has intermediate oxygenation and enzyme activity, not the extremes described.
The portal triad marks the boundary of zone 1, not the hypoxia-prone, high-P450 zone.
Correct — zone 3 is the least oxygenated and richest in P450 enzymes, explaining both its ischemic vulnerability and its role in drug-toxin metabolism.
exp: Hepatic acinar zone 3 (centrilobular, nearest the central vein) receives blood last after passing zones 1 and 2, making it relatively hypoxic and first to suffer ischemic injury (centrilobular necrosis); it also has the highest cytochrome P450 concentration, explaining its vulnerability in paracetamol/acetaminophen toxicity.

subject: Anatomy
q: Melanocytes, the adrenal medulla, and the dorsal root ganglia all arise embryologically from which structure?
why: Mesoderm gives rise to muscle, bone, connective tissue, and the urogenital system, not melanocytes or the adrenal medulla.
Correct — melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and dorsal root ganglia are all classic neural crest derivatives.
Endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the gut and its derivative organs (liver, pancreas, thyroid follicular cells), not these structures.
Surface ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis, hair, nails, and lens, not neural crest derivatives.
exp: The neural crest is a transient, pluripotent cell population arising at the dorsal neural tube margin during neurulation. Its derivatives include melanocytes, adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells), dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, and much of the craniofacial skeleton — a favorite exam theme.

subject: Anatomy
q: What is the most common anatomical position of the vermiform appendix?
why: Pelvic is the second most common position, not the most common.
Pre-ileal is an uncommon position.
Correct — retrocecal is the most common appendiceal position.
Subcecal is a less common variant position.
exp: The retrocecal position (behind the caecum) is the most common position of the appendix, found in roughly 60-65% of individuals, followed by the pelvic position — this positional variation explains atypical presentations of appendicitis (e.g., flank pain, positive psoas sign with retrocecal irritation).

subject: Anatomy
q: Entrapment of which nerve beneath the inguinal ligament, near the anterior superior iliac spine, produces meralgia paresthetica — burning pain and numbness over the anterolateral thigh?
opts: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
why: Correct — entrapment of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh at the inguinal ligament is the cause of meralgia paresthetica.
Femoral nerve compromise causes weakness of knee extension and hip flexion plus anterior thigh/medial leg sensory loss, a motor-plus-sensory picture, not this purely sensory syndrome.
Obturator nerve entrapment affects medial thigh sensation and hip adductor strength, a different territory.
Ilioinguinal nerve injury (e.g., post-hernia repair) causes groin/scrotal or labial sensory disturbance, not anterolateral thigh symptoms.
exp: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2-L3) passes beneath or through the inguinal ligament near the ASIS; entrapment here — common in obesity, pregnancy, or tight belts — produces meralgia paresthetica, a purely sensory syndrome without motor weakness.

subject: Anatomy
q: During hysterectomy, the ureter must be carefully identified where it passes close to the uterine artery to avoid inadvertent ligation. What is the anatomical relationship between the two at this point, commonly taught as "water under the bridge"?
opts: The ureter passes anterior and superior to the uterine artery
The ureter and uterine artery run parallel without crossing
The uterine artery passes posterior to the ureter
The ureter passes inferior and posterior to the uterine artery
why: This reverses the actual relationship — the ureter is inferior/posterior, not anterior/superior, to the artery.
The two structures do cross, they do not run parallel without crossing.
This describes the artery's position relative to the ureter but is not the standard phrasing of the relationship, which keeps the ureter as the passive structure passing under the artery.
Correct — the ureter passes inferior and posterior to (under) the uterine artery, the basis of "water under the bridge".
exp: Near the lateral fornix of the vagina, the uterine artery ("bridge") crosses anterior and superior to the ureter ("water") — this crossing point, roughly 1.5-2cm lateral to the cervix, is the site most at risk of inadvertent ureteric injury during hysterectomy clamping of the uterine vessels.

subject: Anatomy
q: The thymus and the inferior parathyroid glands both develop from which pharyngeal pouch?
why: The first pharyngeal pouch forms the middle ear cavity and eustachian tube, not the thymus/parathyroids.
Correct — the third pouch gives rise to the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands.
The second pharyngeal pouch contributes to the palatine tonsil.
The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands and ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells), not the thymus.
exp: The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the thymus (ventral wing) and inferior parathyroid glands (dorsal wing). Because the thymus migrates caudally during descent and drags the inferior parathyroids with it, their final position is more variable than the superior parathyroids (fourth pouch). Failure of this pouch's development underlies DiGeorge syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
q: During thyroidectomy, the recurrent laryngeal nerve is at risk of injury near the inferior thyroid artery. Which statement about its course is correct?
opts: Both the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves loop around the aortic arch
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the subclavian artery, and the right loops around the aortic arch
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery, and the left loops around the aortic arch
Neither recurrent laryngeal nerve has a vascular relationship in the thorax
why: This incorrectly gives both nerves the same (aortic arch) relation, ignoring their asymmetric embryological courses.
This swaps the two nerves' relations — it is the left nerve that loops the aortic arch and the right that loops the subclavian artery, not vice versa.
Correct — right nerve hooks the right subclavian artery, left nerve hooks the aortic arch.
Both nerves do have defined vascular relationships in the thorax/root of the neck, central to their surgical importance.
exp: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the right vagus and hooks under the right subclavian artery; the left branches from the left vagus and hooks under the aortic arch (lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum) — this asymmetry reflects aortic arch development, and both nerves are vulnerable in thyroid/parathyroid surgery.

subject: Anatomy
q: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle is dissected to safely identify the cystic artery before ligation. What are its three boundaries?
opts: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and the inferior margin of the liver
Cystic duct, common bile duct, and the gallbladder fundus
Cystic artery, cystic duct, and the porta hepatis
Common hepatic duct, cystic artery, and the gallbladder body
why: Correct — cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior liver margin are the classic three boundaries of Calot's triangle.
The common bile duct and gallbladder fundus are not boundaries of the triangle as classically defined.
The cystic artery is a content found within the triangle, not one of its boundaries, and the porta hepatis is not a boundary either.
The gallbladder body is not one of the defining boundaries of Calot's triangle.
exp: Calot's triangle is bounded by the cystic duct inferolaterally, the common hepatic duct medially, and the inferior border of the liver superiorly; the cystic artery (typically from the right hepatic artery) usually lies within it — careful dissection here (the "critical view of safety") avoids injuring the CBD or hepatic artery.

subject: Anatomy
q: In the male perineum, the urogenital diaphragm (perineal membrane) is pierced in the midline by which structure?
why: Pudendal nerve runs in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal in the ischiorectal fossa wall, not through the diaphragm midline
Internal pudendal artery similarly travels via the pudendal canal
Ischiorectal fossa is a fat-filled space lateral to the anal canal, not a structure piercing the diaphragm
Correct - the membranous urethra pierces the urogenital diaphragm in the midline
exp: The urogenital diaphragm, stretching between the ischiopubic rami, is pierced in the midline by the membranous urethra (and additionally the vagina in females); it houses the external urethral sphincter and is a key landmark in pelvic floor and urethral trauma.

subject: Anatomy
q: The portal triad at the periphery of a classic hepatic lobule consists of a branch of the hepatic artery, a branch of the portal vein, and:
why: Correct - an interlobular bile duct completes the portal triad
Central vein lies at the centre of the lobule, not in the triad
Hepatic veins drain central veins and lie outside the lobule
Kupffer cells are sinusoidal macrophages, not a triad component
exp: The portal triad (portal tract) contains an interlobular bile duct alongside branches of the hepatic artery and portal vein; blood mixes in the sinusoids and flows toward the central vein at the lobule's centre, opposite in direction to bile flow, which drains toward the triad's bile duct.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which muscle forms the superomedial boundary of the popliteal fossa?
why: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral, not superomedial, boundary.
Correct - semimembranosus forms the superomedial boundary (semitendinosus lies superficial to it).
Lateral head of gastrocnemius forms part of the inferolateral boundary.
Plantaris lies within the fossa but is not a defining boundary.
exp: The popliteal fossa's superomedial boundary is formed by semimembranosus, the superolateral boundary by biceps femoris, and the two inferior boundaries by the medial and lateral heads of gastrocnemius, with popliteus contributing to the floor.

subject: Anatomy
q: The medial border of Hesselbach's triangle is formed by which structure?
why: Inferior epigastric vessels form the lateral, not medial, boundary of the triangle.
Inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary, not the medial one.
Correct - the lateral margin of rectus abdominis forms the medial border of Hesselbach's triangle.
Conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall/floor but is not itself a defining boundary.
exp: Hesselbach's triangle, the site of direct inguinal hernia protrusion, is bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament, with a comparatively weak transversalis fascia floor.

subject: Anatomy
q: The coeliac trunk, arising from the abdominal aorta at the T12 level, divides into which three branches?
opts: Left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries
Left gastric, splenic, and superior mesenteric arteries
Splenic, common hepatic, and inferior mesenteric arteries
Left gastric, common hepatic, and superior mesenteric arteries
why: Correct - the classic trifurcation of the coeliac trunk
Superior mesenteric artery is a separate branch supplying the midgut
Inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut, unrelated to the coeliac trunk
Again wrongly substitutes the superior mesenteric artery
exp: The coeliac trunk, the first major midline branch of the abdominal aorta at T12, trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, supplying foregut derivatives.

subject: Anatomy
q: The superior orbital fissure transmits which of the following cranial nerves?
why: V2 exits via foramen rotundum, V3 via foramen ovale, not the superior orbital fissure
Correct — oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic division, and abducens all traverse the superior orbital fissure
CN VII and VIII pass through the internal acoustic meatus
CN IX, X, XI exit via the jugular foramen
exp: The superior orbital fissure carries CN III, IV, V1, and VI into the orbit — a lesion here (e.g., cavernous sinus thrombosis, orbital apex syndrome) causes ophthalmoplegia with forehead/eye sensory loss; knowing the fissure-by-fissure nerve distribution (SOF vs foramen rotundum vs ovale vs jugular foramen) is a recurring one-liner across papers.

subject: Anatomy
q: The perineum derives its principal arterial supply from a branch of which artery?
opts: Internal iliac artery (via internal pudendal artery)
why: External iliac supplies the lower limb, not the perineum
Superior gluteal artery supplies the gluteal region
Correct — internal pudendal artery, a branch of internal iliac, is the principal supply
Femoral artery is a continuation of external iliac, supplying the lower limb
exp: The internal pudendal artery, the main branch of the internal iliac artery's anterior division, is the principal blood supply to the perineum — it re-enters the perineum via the lesser sciatic foramen after looping through the pudendal (Alcock's) canal alongside the pudendal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which component of levator ani forms a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction, maintaining the anorectal angle and contributing to faecal continence?
why: Iliococcygeus forms a thin pelvic-floor sheet, not the anorectal sling
Correct — puborectalis forms the U-shaped anorectal sling
Pubococcygeus supports the pelvic viscera generally, not specifically the anorectal sling
Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) is not part of levator ani, supports the coccyx
exp: Puborectalis, the most medial part of levator ani, forms a U-shaped sling that pulls the anorectal junction anteriorly, creating the anorectal angle (approximately 90 degrees at rest) essential for faecal continence; voluntary relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens this angle.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which thyroid cell type, located within or adjacent to the follicular epithelium, secretes calcitonin in response to hypercalcemia?
why: Follicular epithelial cells synthesize thyroglobulin and secrete T3/T4, not calcitonin
Oxyphil cells are found in the parathyroid, not the thyroid
Correct — parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin
Chief cells are the PTH-secreting cells of the parathyroid, functionally opposite to calcitonin
exp: Parafollicular (C) cells, derived embryologically from the neural crest (via the ultimobranchial body), lie within the thyroid follicular basement membrane and secrete calcitonin, which lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption — these are the cells of origin for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

subject: Anatomy
q: Structures traversing the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus include all EXCEPT:
why: CN III runs in the lateral wall
CN IV runs in the lateral wall
Correct exception - CN VI runs freely within the body of the sinus
V1 runs in the lateral wall
exp: Within the cavernous sinus, CN III, IV, and V1 (and sometimes V2) run in the lateral wall, while CN VI runs freely through the body of the sinus alongside the internal carotid artery - this explains why isolated abducens nerve palsy is often the earliest sign of cavernous sinus pathology such as thrombosis or fistula.

subject: Anatomy
q: During an emergency venous cutdown at the ankle, the great saphenous vein is most reliably located at which landmark?
why: The short saphenous vein, not the great saphenous, runs posterior to the lateral malleolus
The popliteal fossa contains the popliteal vein/artery, not the superficial great saphenous vein
Correct — reliable venous cutdown landmark
The small saphenous vein runs near the Achilles tendon, not the great saphenous
exp: The great saphenous vein runs consistently anterior to the medial malleolus at the ankle, making this the standard emergency venous cutdown site when peripheral IV access has failed.

subject: Anatomy
q: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) exits the skull through which foramen?
why: Foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2), not the mandibular division
Correct — foramen ovale transmits V3
Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery/vein plus the nervus spinosus (V3's recurrent meningeal branch) — but the V3 trunk itself exits via foramen ovale
Jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein, unrelated to V3
exp: The mandibular nerve (V3), the only trigeminal division carrying both sensory and motor fibres to muscles of mastication, exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen ovale — distinguishing it from V1 (superior orbital fissure) and V2 (foramen rotundum).

subject: Anatomy
q: Rupture of the penile (bulbar) urethra deep to Buck's fascia allows urine to extravasate into a space bounded by which layer, sparing the thighs?
why: Camper's fascia is the superficial fatty layer of the anterior abdominal wall, not perineal
Denonvilliers' fascia is the rectovesical septum, unrelated
Scarpa's fascia is the abdominal wall counterpart reached via continuity, but the perineal barrier itself is Colles'
Correct, Colles' fascia is the perineal membrane's superficial continuation, fused to the fascia lata
exp: Colles' fascia attaches to the pubic arch and perineal body and fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh - this is why extravasated urine from a ruptured bulbar urethra classically spares the thighs but balloons the scrotum, penis, and lower abdominal wall.

subject: Anatomy
q: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by which structure?
why: Wrong — adductor longus's medial border forms the medial boundary, not the lateral one.
Wrong — the inguinal ligament forms the superior boundary (base), not the lateral side.
Correct — the lateral boundary is the medial border of sartorius.
Wrong — gracilis does not form any boundary of the femoral triangle.
exp: The femoral triangle's boundaries: superiorly, the inguinal ligament (base); medially, the medial border of adductor longus; laterally, the medial border of sartorius; floor, pectineus/adductor longus/iliopsoas; roof, fascia lata. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, artery, vein, lymphatics (mnemonic NAVeL).

subject: Anatomy
q: The proximal convoluted tubule is lined by which epithelium, distinguishing it histologically from the distal convoluted tubule?
opts: Simple cuboidal epithelium without a brush border
Simple cuboidal epithelium with a prominent brush border
why: Wrong — absence of a brush border describes the DCT, not the PCT.
Wrong — simple squamous epithelium lines Bowman's capsule's parietal layer and the thin limb of the loop of Henle, not the PCT.
Wrong — transitional epithelium lines the urinary tract from renal pelvis to urethra, not the tubules.
Correct — PCT cells are cuboidal with a brush border that makes the lumen look indistinct.
exp: The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal cells with a prominent apical brush border (microvilli, for reabsorption) and eosinophilic, mitochondria-rich cytoplasm, giving the lumen a fuzzy, indistinct appearance on light microscopy. The DCT is also simple cuboidal but without a brush border, giving a clearer lumen and more distinct cell boundaries — the key histological differentiator on a kidney slide.

subject: Anatomy
q: The floor of the inguinal canal is formed predominantly by which structure?
why: Wrong — the conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially, not the floor.
Wrong — the external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the canal, not the floor.
Correct — the floor is formed by the inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
Wrong — transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall, not the floor.
exp: The inguinal canal's walls: anterior wall, external oblique aponeurosis (reinforced laterally by internal oblique); posterior wall, transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon); roof, arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis; floor, the inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.

subject: Anatomy
q: McBurney's point, the classic site of maximal tenderness in acute appendicitis, lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the umbilicus to which landmark?
why: Correct — the line runs from the umbilicus to the right ASIS; McBurney's point is at the junction of its lateral one-third and medial two-thirds.
The midpoint of the inguinal ligament is a different surface landmark (overlying the femoral artery), a classic point of confusion with McBurney's point.
The pubic tubercle marks the superficial inguinal ring, not McBurney's point.
The iliac crest is not the landmark used in this classic surface marking.
exp: McBurney's point = junction of the lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of a line joining the umbilicus to the right ASIS; it marks the base of the appendix and is the classic site of maximal tenderness in acute appendicitis. Do not confuse it with the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (site of the femoral artery pulse) — a frequent distractor.

subject: Anatomy
q: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels re-enter the perineum by travelling through which fascial canal along the lateral wall of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa?
why: Correct — Alcock's canal, formed by a split in obturator internus fascia, is the specific conduit within the ischiorectal fossa
The inguinal canal transmits the spermatic cord/round ligament, unrelated
The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve/vessels to the medial thigh
The greater sciatic foramen is where the pudendal nerve first exits the pelvis around the ischial spine, before entering the pudendal canal
exp: The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) runs along the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa within a split of the obturator internus fascia, carrying the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels forward to the perineum — the anatomical basis for pudendal block landmarks and Alcock's canal syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
q: The stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium lining the oesophagus abruptly transitions to simple columnar epithelium at which landmark?
why: The pylorus is the gastroduodenal junction, both sides already columnar
The pharyngoesophageal junction is squamous on both sides
Correct — the Z-line marks the abrupt squamous-to-columnar switch
The duodenojejunal flexure is columnar on both sides
exp: The oesophagus is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium throughout and switches abruptly to simple columnar (gastric) epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction, seen endoscopically as the irregular Z-line — the landmark relevant to Barrett's oesophagus, where this line shifts proximally with columnar metaplasia.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder, allowing it to withstand distension during filling?
why: Simple cuboidal lines structures like renal tubules and small ducts, not an organ needing to stretch
Correct — transitional epithelium is unique to the urinary passages for this reason
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar lines the respiratory tract and vas deferens, not the bladder
Nonkeratinized stratified squamous lines the oesophagus, vagina, and distal anal canal
exp: The urinary tract from renal pelvis to proximal urethra is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium whose umbrella cells flatten and whose layer thins as the bladder distends, then thickens again when empty - the histological basis of bladder capacity.

subject: Anatomy
q: The portal vein is formed by the union of which two veins behind the neck of the pancreas?
opts: Splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein
Superior mesenteric vein and inferior mesenteric vein
Superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein
why: Incorrect pairing — the IMV typically drains into the splenic vein but does not itself form the portal vein
SMV plus IMV is not the classic description of portal vein formation
Gastric veins drain into the portal system but do not form the portal vein trunk
Correct — SMV plus splenic vein behind the pancreatic neck
exp: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein (the inferior mesenteric vein usually joins the splenic vein just before this confluence) — a key surgical landmark in pancreatic and portal procedures.

subject: Anatomy
q: What type of epithelium lines the trachea?
opts: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells
why: Correct - the classic respiratory epithelium lining the trachea
Simple columnar epithelium lines the GI tract, not the trachea
Stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium lines the oesophagus and vocal cords, not the trachea proper
Transitional epithelium lines the urinary tract, not the airway
exp: The trachea and most of the lower respiratory tract (except the vocal cords) are lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with interspersed goblet cells - the classic respiratory epithelium. This is a frequent image-based histology identification question in NEET PG.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which foramen at the base of the skull transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves along with the internal jugular vein?
why: Foramen ovale carries the mandibular nerve (V3) and accessory meningeal artery, not IX-XI
Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein
Correct - jugular foramen carries CN IX, X, XI and the jugular bulb/internal jugular vein
Hypoglossal canal transmits only CN XII
exp: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X, and XI along with the sigmoid sinus, which continues as the internal jugular vein - a frequently asked base-of-skull foramen contents question.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which nerve passes through the foramen rotundum to exit the middle cranial fossa?
why: V3 exits through foramen ovale, not foramen rotundum
Correct - foramen rotundum transmits V2 (maxillary nerve)
V1 passes through the superior orbital fissure
Facial nerve exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen
exp: The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) from the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion into the pterygopalatine fossa; V3 exits via foramen ovale, V1 via the superior orbital fissure, and the facial nerve via the stylomastoid foramen - a commonly confused set of skull-base exit points.

subject: Anatomy
q: Tearing of which midline fibromuscular structure during childbirth predisposes to anal sphincter injury and faecal incontinence?
why: The ischial spine is a bony landmark for pudendal block and labour station, not a muscle attachment site.
Correct - the perineal body is the fibromuscular node where bulbospongiosus, external anal sphincter, and transverse perinei converge.
Alcock's canal transmits the pudendal nerve and vessels, unrelated to perineal body function.
The sacrospinous ligament separates the greater and lesser sciatic foramina and has no role in perineal body integrity.
exp: The perineal body (central tendon of perineum) is the fibromuscular node where bulbospongiosus, external anal sphincter, and superficial/deep transverse perinei muscles converge. Its damage in childbirth (or a poorly repaired episiotomy) predisposes to anal sphincter disruption and faecal incontinence.

subject: Anatomy
q: Through which foramen does the facial nerve exit the skull after traversing the facial canal?
why: Jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX, X, XI and the internal jugular vein, not the facial nerve's exit point
Correct — the facial nerve exits the skull here after running through the facial (Fallopian) canal, just posterior to the styloid process
Foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), not the facial nerve
Internal acoustic meatus is where the facial nerve enters (with the vestibulocochlear nerve) to begin its intrapetrous course, not where it exits
exp: The facial nerve's course: internal acoustic meatus (entry) to facial canal (with its genu, giving off greater petrosal nerve, nerve to stapedius, and chorda tympani) to stylomastoid foramen (exit) — a key landmark for facial nerve identification in parotidectomy.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which muscle forms the principal component of the pelvic diaphragm and is most vulnerable to stretch injury during vaginal delivery?
exp: Levator ani (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) forms the pelvic diaphragm; its pubovisceral fibers stretch the most during vaginal delivery, predisposing to pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence later in life.

subject: Anatomy
q: A Meckel diverticulum, the classic overall commonest pathologic lead point for childhood intussusception, arises from incomplete obliteration of which embryonic structure?
why: Wrong: the urachus is the allantoic remnant forming the median umbilical ligament, from bladder to umbilicus.
Correct: Meckel diverticulum is a persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct on the antimesenteric ileal border.
Wrong: the processus vaginalis relates to testicular descent and inguinal hernia.
Wrong: the allantois relates to bladder and urachus development, not the vitelline duct.
exp: Meckel diverticulum is a true diverticulum (contains all bowel wall layers) arising from a persistent omphalomesenteric/vitelline duct, which normally obliterates by the 7th week of gestation. Remember the rule of 2s: ~2% of the population, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve, ~2 inches long, presents by age 2 when symptomatic, and may contain 2 types of ectopic tissue (gastric or pancreatic) - ectopic gastric mucosa is the one that causes painless lower GI bleeding via peptic ulceration.

subject: Anatomy
q: Injury to the common peroneal (fibular) nerve at the neck of the fibula most characteristically produces which clinical sign?
opts: Foot drop with loss of dorsiflexion and eversion
Loss of plantarflexion with clawing of toes
exp: The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, making it the most commonly injured lower-limb nerve (plaster casts, fibular fractures, prolonged squatting/leg-crossing); injury causes foot drop from loss of dorsiflexors (deep peroneal) and evertors (superficial peroneal), with a characteristic high-stepping gait.

subject: Anatomy
q: The transpyloric plane of Addison, an important surface landmark for abdominal viscera, lies at the level of the lower border of which vertebra?
why: T12 is too high; the subcostal and transpyloric planes lie lower
Correct: the transpyloric plane lies at the lower border of L1
L2 is below the transpyloric plane and has no named plane in this series
L3 is the level of the subcostal plane, not the transpyloric plane
exp: The transpyloric plane (of Addison) lies at the lower border of L1 and marks the pylorus, the neck of the pancreas, the duodenojejunal flexure, the hila of both kidneys, the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the formation of the portal vein — a favourite single-image landmark question.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structures lie within the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament), forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow?
opts: Splenic artery, splenic vein, and pancreatic duct
Superior mesenteric artery, vein, and inferior vena cava
Portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and common bile duct
Left gastric artery, right gastric artery, and cystic duct
why: Splenic vessels and the pancreatic duct lie behind the stomach with the pancreas
SMA, SMV and IVC are retroperitoneal, not in the hepatoduodenal ligament
Correct: the portal vein, hepatic artery proper and common bile duct run in the free edge
The gastric arteries run along the lesser curvature, not the free edge, and the cystic duct is not part of the triad
exp: The free edge of the lesser omentum carries the portal triad: common bile duct (right anterior), hepatic artery proper (left anterior), and portal vein (posterior, between the two) — remembered as duct right, artery left, vein behind. This free edge is the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow, which connects the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs; the inferior vena cava lies posterior to the foramen, not within the free edge itself.

subject: Anatomy
q: During a pudendal nerve block for vaginal delivery or episiotomy, which bony landmark is used to guide needle placement, as the nerve hooks around it?
why: Correct: the ischial spine is felt per vaginam and is where the pudendal nerve hooks round
The ischial tuberosity is not where the nerve crosses and does not guide the transvaginal block
The pubic symphysis is anterior and unrelated to the nerve
The sacral promontory is a pelvic inlet landmark unrelated to the block
exp: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, then re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen to travel in the pudendal (Alcock's) canal. The ischial spine is palpated transvaginally and is the key landmark for the transvaginal pudendal nerve block used during labour/episiotomy repair.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structure distinguishes a direct from an indirect inguinal hernia at operation?
why: Correct: indirect sacs lie lateral and direct hernias medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
The superficial epigastric vein is a superficial tributary unrelated to the deep ring
The ilioinguinal nerve runs with the cord but does not separate the two types
The conjoint tendon forms part of the posterior wall but is not the dividing landmark
exp: An indirect hernia sac lies lateral to the inferior epigastric artery (through the deep ring); a direct hernia bulges medial to it through Hesselbach triangle. This is the single landmark that settles the distinction intra-operatively.

subject: Anatomy
q: Injury to which nerve produces winging of the scapula?
why: Correct: the long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior, and its palsy gives medial winging
Axillary nerve injury weakens the deltoid and numbs the regimental badge area, with no winging
Thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi; injury weakens adduction and extension, not scapular fixation
Suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; injury weakens abduction and lateral rotation
exp: The long thoracic nerve (C5,6,7) supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall. Its loss gives medial winging, classically after axillary surgery or a blow to the lateral chest.

subject: Anatomy
q: Which structure passes through the foramen spinosum?
why: Mandibular nerve leaves through the foramen ovale
Internal carotid artery enters through the carotid canal
Correct: foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery (with its vein and the meningeal branch of V3)
Facial nerve leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen
exp: Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery; the mandibular nerve leaves through the adjacent foramen ovale. This is the artery torn in an extradural haematoma after a pterion fracture.
